c.tagline: Mexico's golden-age Pacific bay resort - cliff divers, beaches and nightlife - rebuilding after Hurricane Otis.

taxi.fareNote: Acapulco taxis are not metered and charge by zone - agree the fare before getting in. Uber and DiDi operate and are usually cheaper and safer, though taxi drivers sometimes restrict app pickups at the airport.

emergency.note: 911 is Mexico's unified emergency number for police, fire and ambulance; 078 is the national tourist assistance line.

avoid.reason: Stay out of non-tourist colonias such as Ciudad Renacimiento, Emiliano Zapata and Jardín, and the city's outskirts, where cartel-related violence is concentrated.
Stick to the Zona Dorada and Diamante hotel strips at night, avoid beaches after dark, and use hotel-arranged or app taxis.

hood_desc: The classic 'golden zone' along the Costera Miguel Aleman, lined with mid-century high-rise hotels, beach clubs, restaurants and Acapulco's famous nightlife, right on the main sweep of the bay; the busiest and most convenient base, though still recovering from Hurricane Otis.

Punta Diamante, the newer luxury zone southeast of the bay, with gated high-rise condos, big resorts, golf courses and the long Revolcadero surf beach; quieter and more polished than the Costera, but spread out and reliant on taxis.

Old Acapulco around the Zocalo, the Fort of San Diego and the small, calm Caleta and Caletilla beaches, plus the legendary La Quebrada cliff divers; the most historic, atmospheric and budget-friendly part of town.

A sheltered cove southeast of the main bay, known for its calm swimming, waterfront seafood palapas and a handful of upscale hotels tucked into the hills; a mellower, scenic alternative to the Costera.

A long, laid-back sandbar northwest of the city between the ocean and Coyuca Lagoon, famous for its dramatic Pacific sunsets, horseback riding and low-key beachfront guesthouses; the most relaxed, rustic stretch.

water.note: Drink bottled or purified water only, as locals do.

transit.hours: Buses and colectivos run roughly 05:00 to around 23:00 along the main Costera corridor, with far fewer after dark, when taxis or ride apps are the norm.
transit.note: Acapulco has no metro or rail; getting around means the cheap buses and colectivo vans along the Costera Miguel Aleman, taxis, or ride-hailing apps. Note the city is still rebuilding tourism infrastructure after Hurricane Otis struck in October 2023.
transit.pay: City buses and colectivo vans are paid in cash to the driver (roughly MXN 10-12 a ride); there is no rechargeable transit card. Many visitors ride the buses that run the length of the Costera between Old Acapulco and the Zona Dorada.

landmarks: La Quebrada Cliff Divers
Fearless clavadistas plunge 35 metres from a narrow clifftop into a surging Pacific inlet, a death-defying Acapulco spectacle performed daily since 1934.
Fuerte de San Diego
A star-shaped 17th-century Spanish fortress that repelled pirates and guarded Manila galleon treasure, now housing the excellent Acapulco Historical Museum.
Playa Condesa
The golden heart of Acapulco Bay's hotel strip, where parasailers drift above lively beach clubs against a backdrop of glittering high-rises.
Isla de la Roqueta
A short boat hop across the bay, this green islet offers snorkelling coves, a lighthouse hike, and glass-bottom boat views of the submerged Virgin of Guadalupe statue.
Capilla de la Paz (Chapel of Peace)
A minimalist hilltop chapel crowned by a towering white cross, its gardens delivering the most sweeping panorama of Acapulco Bay's glittering crescent.
Zocalo and Nuestra Senora de la Soledad Cathedral
Acapulco's shady old-town plaza hums beneath banyan trees before a quirky cathedral whose blue Byzantine-style domes resemble a Moorish mosque.
Sinfonia del Mar
An open-air amphitheatre of curving stone terraces spilling toward the Pacific, purpose-built for applauding Acapulco's famously fiery sunsets.
Playas Caleta y Caletilla
Twin gentle-watered coves beloved since Acapulco's golden Hollywood era, still the favourite family beaches with calm swimming and old-school seafood palapas.
Pie de la Cuesta
A rustic beach strip northwest of town famed for thundering surf, horseback rides, and Mexico's most theatrical sunsets over an endless Pacific horizon.
Laguna de Coyuca
A palm-fringed freshwater lagoon where boat tours glide past mangroves, water birds, and film locations from Rambo and Tarzan movies.

train.note: No passenger railway serves Acapulco - the old Mexico City line closed long ago and the network here is freight-only. Arrive on the Autopista del Sol toll road by coach or car, or fly in.

bus.note: No international coaches. Estrella de Oro (https://www.estrelladeoro.com.mx/) and Costa Line/Estrella Blanca run from the Ejido and Papagayo terminals to Mexico City in about 5 hours on the toll road and along the coast to Zihuatanejo and Puerto Escondido. Check current security advice for the coastal highway before travelling at night.

ferry.note: There is no scheduled passenger ferry from Acapulco. The bay has glass-bottomed boats to Roqueta island and sunset cruises, which are excursions rather than transport, and the port takes occasional cruise calls.

half.name: Tres Palos Lagoon
half.blurb: Coastal lagoon with boat rides through an Afro-Mexican fishing village, a turtle hatchery, and a crocodile sanctuary.

full.name: Taxco
full.blurb: Colonial hill town famed for silver workshops, whitewashed streets, and the baroque Santa Prisca church.

full.name: Mexico City
full.blurb: The national capital's historic center and the pyramids of Teotihuacan, reached via the toll highway through the mountains.
